# Trajectory Prediction Under Sensor Degradation

Predicting where NFL players will be 1.9 seconds after a pass is thrown — and,
more interestingly, **measuring which prediction methods survive when the
tracking sensor gets worse.**

The dataset is NFL Next Gen Stats, a UWB installation reporting positions at
10 Hz. NFL Football Operations states only that the system *"charts individual
movements within inches"* — it publishes no numeric accuracy figure
([operations.nfl.com/gameday/technology/nfl-next-gen-stats](https://operations.nfl.com/gameday/technology/nfl-next-gen-stats)).
This project measured the published position stream directly rather than
assume a number: it is quantized to 0.01 yd, with no detectable white noise
above that step (see Methodology). Every result here is framed as *"what
happens to this method when you deploy it on cheaper hardware"* — but `σ=0`
in every experiment below means *this already-processed stream*, not raw
sensor output. See the note in Methodology before reading any crossing as a
statement about the real sensor.

For the full Part 1 physics-study detail (Tier 0a/0b, every baseline, the
Kalman/IMM/hybrid family, the coverage-guard failure and its fix, the R-convention
adoption) — see [PART1_DETAIL.md](PART1_DETAIL.md).

---

**TL;DR**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Best accuracy, held-out test** | a small GRU, **1.80 yd** @1.9 s — vs **4.18 yd** for the best physics baseline |
| **But** | that same model is unusable at σ = 0.2 yd of added noise — on top of an already-processed stream, not raw sensor output |
| **Fix** | noise-augmented training; the learned model then beats physics out to **σ = 0.93 yd** |
| **Mechanism** | the network learns a velocity gain of **~8.8** where physics gives **1.90** — a 4.6× amplifier pointed at the noisiest channel in the dataset |

![Animated single play: actual player positions vs. a constant velocity baseline prediction, while the ball is in the air.](outputs/play_animation.gif)

One play — the longest ball flight in the dataset, chosen because the
motion is clearest at that length — over 4.0 s. The gap between the
filled (actual) and open (constant velocity) circles is what every
number in this document is trying to shrink.

The project's actual deliverable is not an accuracy number. It is a measured
answer to **"when should I use a learned model and when should I use a
Kalman filter?"**

---

[README.md > The question]
Standard trajectory-prediction work ranks methods on clean data. This project
asks a different question:

> A tracking system's accuracy is a hardware purchasing decision. If I spend
> less on anchors, or deploy in a worse RF environment, **which of these
> methods degrades gracefully and which one falls off a cliff?**

So every experiment has the same shape: inject σ yards of Gaussian noise into
the player positions, recompute everything downstream, and measure the error
curve. σ = 0 is the control, and it means *no noise added on top of the
published NGS stream* — not *raw sensor output*, and not *noise-free*. That
stream is itself already quantized to 0.01 yd and vendor-processed (see
Methodology); every σ in this project is noise added on top of whatever
processing already happened before the data was published, not total sensor
noise. A reader who assumes σ=0 means raw UWB will misread every number
below.

[README.md > Why the learned model breaks]
Velocity is not measured; it is computed by differencing adjacent positions:

```
v[t] = (x[t] − x[t−1]) / Δt
```

With Δt = 0.1 s, this amplifies position noise by `√2/Δt ≈ 14×`. At σ = 0.2 yd
the velocity feature carries 2.83 yd/s of noise against true speeds of
3–8 yd/s — the *direction* of the velocity vector is essentially randomised.

Physics integrates that channel with a gain fixed at the horizon (1.9 s).
The network's gain is whatever training found optimal, and in training the
velocity channel was reliable:

| | velocity gain | vs physics |
|---|---|---|
| physics (integration) | 1.90 | 1.0× |
| K3 (clean training input) | **~8.8** (8.78–8.89) | ~4.6× |
| K4 (Kalman-filtered input) | 1.6–2.1 | ~0.8–1.1× |
| K5 (noise-augmented) | 0.46–0.56 | ~0.24–0.29× |

Monotonic, in the predicted direction, and **nothing here was hand-tuned** —
each gain emerged from training.

> **A learned model calibrates its sensitivity to each input according to that
> input's reliability during training. When deployment reliability changes,
> the learned gain is wrong — and nothing in the model knows it.**

A Kalman filter has `R` for exactly this. You read the new sensor's spec off
the datasheet and change one number. There is no equivalent for a trained
network short of retraining.

K3's soft failure threshold is σ = 0.00276 — below the published data's own
0.01 yd quantization step (see Methodology). A model with a gain of 8.8 fails
at a noise level the data cannot even represent. Monitoring cannot cover for
that; the model has to be fixed.

---

[README.md > Part 1 — the physics study]
Six closed-form baselines, then Kalman / constant-acceleration / IMM filters,
then a hybrid. The unifying concept is **baseline length**:

```
angular error ≈ measurement noise / baseline length
```

| direction source | baseline | angular error |
|---|---|---|
| differencing adjacent frames | 0.6 yd | ±33° |
| bearing to the ball's landing point | 25 yd | ±0.6° |

![Mean displacement error vs. time since the throw, for all 11 physics-only baselines, clean data.](outputs/error_curves.png)

`constant_position` (orange) — no velocity at all — diverges fastest and
worst; every baseline that uses velocity clusters well below it.

Four findings:

1. **Filtering is a losing trade on clean data, and when it stops being one
   depends on which baseline you ask.** Isolating the cost of smoothing
   alone — `tbl_kalman_speed` vs. `toward_ball_land`, identical except for
   where speed comes from (Kalman posterior vs. NGS's own reported speed),
   measured on held-out clean data — costs **0.77 yd**.
   - `tbl_kalman_speed` vs. **`constant_velocity`** crosses at **σ = 0.075**:
     the hybrid is worth it in place of the simplest baseline almost
     immediately as noise is added.
   - `tbl_kalman_speed` vs. **`toward_ball_land`** — the same-direction,
     speed-only isolation above — crosses at **σ = 0.1432** (95% CI
     0.1355–0.1513). What this means relative to the real sensor's own
     accuracy is unknown — see Methodology on why no such comparison can be
     supported from this data. The crossing itself, and the 0.77 yd cost
     below it, stand as measurements.
2. **Differentiation amplification.** `constant_velocity` degrades 37.7×; the
   hybrid degrades 1.8×.

[README.md > Methodology]
This is the part worth reading if you are evaluating the engineering rather
than the football.

**What `σ=0` actually is, and what the sensor's real noise actually is.**
NFL Football Operations publishes no numeric accuracy figure for NGS — only
that it *"charts individual movements within inches."* This project measured
the published position stream directly rather than carry forward an assumed
number. Three checks, cheapest first: (1) `x`/`y` in the raw files are exact
multiples of 0.01 yd, no exceptions; (2) the distribution of `x[t]-x[t-1]` is
discrete — 100.00% of successive differences land exactly on the 0.01 grid,
nothing in between; (3) an estimator built to detect additive noise (a
difference-order ladder, validated end-to-end by injecting a known σ=0.10
into real motion and recovering 0.1001) finds no white noise above the
quantization step in the real data. **Conclusion: the published stream is
quantized to 0.01 yd and carries no detectable sensor noise above that — not
because the sensor is that precise (no UWB system achieves millimetre
accuracy), but because whatever noise the raw sensor has was removed before
publication.** `σ=0` in every experiment in this project means *this
already-processed stream*, not raw sensor output, and every σ>0 is noise
added on top of it, not total sensor noise. No comparison of a measured
crossing to "the sensor's accuracy" is supported by this data, and none is
made below. Full measurement detail, including the PSD check and why its
apparent high-frequency rolloff turned out to be a windowing artifact (caught
by re-running it on synthetic white noise before trusting it) rather than
evidence either way, is in PART1_DETAIL.md.

The apparent rolloff above ~1 Hz is a windowing artifact, not measured
sensor noise, confirmed by re-running this same check on synthetic white
noise before trusting it. This figure alone is inconclusive; the
quantization check above it is decisive.

**Splits by game, not by play.** Plays within a game share players and
schemes; a play-level split leaks that structure. 272 games → 190 train /
41 val / 41 test, fixed by seed, IDs written to disk.

**5-fold grouped cross-validation** over the 231 train+val games for all
development decisions. Every play receives an out-of-fold prediction, and the
fold-to-fold spread is a free error bar.

**The K5/physics crossing sigma is a play-level bootstrap estimate**
(1,000 resamples, seed 0), which is what the point estimate and 95% CI
quoted above come from. An independent estimator — linear interpolation on
the aggregate mean-error curves — gives 0.921 on the same test split,
consistent with the bootstrap estimate and well inside its interval.

**That crossing was checked against all 13 physics baselines, not just the
three plotted.** Only 3 had ever been scored under noise on the test split;
the other 10 (`scripts/run_tier1_test_degrade_allbaselines.py`) hadn't. `tbl_kalman_speed`
turns out to be the pointwise-best baseline at every σ across the entire

the full 13-baseline envelope is identical to the one reported — not just
close, bit-for-bit identical, because the envelope and `tbl_kalman_speed`
are the same curve there.

**A coverage guard that actually fires.** Only ~3.5% of plays have a ball
flight reaching 3 seconds. The project's original headline horizon was 3 s —
measured, at one point, on 24 tracks. `MIN_COVERAGE` existed in the config but
was wired only into the plotting path. The primary horizon is now 1.9 s
(53% coverage) and every reported number carries its coverage.

> A guard that only fires on plots is not a guard.

![Track coverage percentage vs. time since the throw, with the chosen 1.9s primary horizon and the old 3s headline horizon marked.](outputs/horizon_coverage.png)

Coverage falls off sharply after 1.5s; the old 3s headline horizon
covers just 3.5% of tracks, which is why this project's primary horizon
is 1.9s (53% coverage) instead.

times worse.** A model with access to the answer does not lose anywhere.

reported at all. A good number without a mechanism is as untrustworthy as an

# Trajectory prediction under degraded sensing

Short-horizon multi-target trajectory prediction on 10 Hz UWB player
tracking data (NFL Next Gen Stats), comparing model-based estimation
against learned sequence models and characterising how each degrades as
the sensing quality drops.

**Status: Tier 1 Part 1 — sensor degradation sweep complete. Run on the
real 2023 season data; see [Results](#results) below.**

---

[PART1_DETAIL.md > The question]
At the moment the ball leaves the quarterback's hand, given every player's
position, speed and heading up to that instant, where will the tracked
players be while the ball is in the air?

The interesting quantity is not the accuracy number. It is the split:

- **How much of player motion is explained by physics alone?**
  A body with a position and a velocity keeps going. That costs nothing to
  compute and it accounts for some of the motion.
- **How much is explained by intent?**
  A receiver running a route, a defender reacting to the throw — that is
  not physics, and no filter recovers it. It has to be learned.

Tier 0 measures the first so that later tiers can measure the second.
Without a physics floor, a learned model's error is a number with nothing
to compare it against.

[PART1_DETAIL.md > Roadmap]
| Tier | Content | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 0a | Data pipeline, physics baselines, animation | error-vs-horizon curve |
| 0b | Kalman / IMM filter, state estimation | filter vs naive extrapolation |
| 1 | Learned sequence model + sensing degradation study | robustness curves |
| 2 | Streaming inference, quantisation, latency benchmark | latency vs accuracy |

[PART1_DETAIL.md > Why UWB matters here]
Next Gen Stats positions come from ultra-wideband tags in the players'
shoulder pads, read by receivers around the stadium at roughly 10 Hz. They
are measurements, not ground truth: every sample carries localisation
error, and coverage degrades when bodies occlude a tag.

Three consequences shape the project:

1. **Velocity estimated by differencing positions amplifies that error**,
   because the sampling interval is small. Standard motivation for a state
   estimator, and the reason Tier 0b exists.
2. **Sensing quality is a variable, not a constant.** Tier 1 treats it as
   one: inject localisation noise, drop samples, reduce the update rate,
   and measure the accuracy cost. That trade-off curve is the main result.
3. **The ball's landing point is itself an estimate.** It is supplied as an
   exact input here, but a live system would infer it from the same noisy
   tracking stream — so error in the landing point is a second degradation
   axis, and one the baselines below are directly sensitive to.

[PART1_DETAIL.md > Baselines]
| Predictor | Assumption |
|---|---|
| `constant_position` | nobody moves — the absolute floor |
| `constant_velocity` | current velocity holds |
| `constant_acceleration` | current acceleration holds |
| `damped_velocity` | velocity decays with a fixed time constant |
| `toward_ball_land` | run straight at the landing spot at current speed |
| `velocity_turning_to_ball` | momentum early, destination late |

Two comparisons carry most of the information:

`constant_acceleration` against `constant_velocity` locates where a purely
kinematic description stops holding. Nobody sustains their instantaneous
acceleration for three seconds, so the quadratic term diverges; the
crossover point is a result, not a bug.

`toward_ball_land` against `constant_velocity` separates *where a player is
going* from *where they are pointed*. The first uses only the destination
and ignores heading; the second the reverse. Where the destination-only
baseline wins, intent is already legible in the geometry — and a learned
model has to beat that, not just beat constant velocity.

`{CB,DE,DT,FB,FS,ILB,MLB,NT,OLB,QB,RB,S,SS,TE,WR}` — this competition's data
excludes linemen). Used `player_role=="Passer"` (the QB) and the earliest
frames of each play as the best available substitute, swept window length
5 to 25 frames. Both a successive-difference and a detrended-residual
estimator were run; they disagreed by 20-170% depending on window length,
and grew with window length in both directions — small windows biased the
detrended estimator toward zero (fitting a line through 3-5 points
absorbs real variation into the trend), large windows picked up genuine
motion (the autocorrelation of residuals at 15-25 frames showed the
smooth, slowly-decaying signature of unremoved curvature, not noise).
**Abandoned**: there is no window in this dataset's tracked history that is
both long enough to detrend reliably and short enough to still be
stationary.

**Attempt 2: difference-order ladder, no stationarity assumed.** Real
motion is smooth; sensor noise is white; differencing is a high-pass
filter. For white noise of variance σ², the n-th order difference has

text:
[PART1_DETAIL.md > Design notes]
**Play direction is normalised.** Leftward plays are mirrored so every play
runs in `+x`. The mirroring has to reach the output file and the ball
landing point too — the output file carries no `play_direction` column of
its own, so the flag is joined from the input. Missing either produces a
pipeline that looks healthy and scores nonsense.

**Acceleration is projected onto the current heading.** NGS gives `a` as a
magnitude with no direction. Treating it as along-track is exact when a
player accelerates in a straight line and wrong when they cut — which is
precisely why the constant-acceleration baseline fails on turns.

**Every predictor shares one signature** —
`f(sample, horizon) -> (n_players, horizon, 2)`, where `sample` is a
`data_loader.PlaySample`. The six baselines above only ever touch
`sample.state` (the anchor frame); Kalman and IMM are the first predictors
that also read `sample.history` (every pre-throw frame per player). The
signature carries the whole sample, rather than just the state frame, so
that dependency is visible in the function itself instead of hidden behind
a side channel.

Next Gen Stats positions come from UWB tags in players' shoulder pads, read
by stadium receivers at ~10 Hz. That is a fact about the data, not a
rhetorical device.

But the *motivation* is separate from the *content*, and conflating them
produces something Roy cannot say honestly in an interview. The honest
version: he is a football fan who wanted a project with real tracking data;
what makes it technically interesting is that the data is a UWB
localisation system's output, so it can be treated as a state-estimation
problem with a sensing-degradation study attached.

Roy had not encountered UWB before this project started. If the framing
ever starts to feel like a stretch, the fallback is to keep every
experiment and simply not invoke UWB — "model-based filters vs learned
sequence models for multi-target trajectory prediction" stands on its own.
The code does not change either way. This decision can be deferred
indefinitely.

**Scope is deliberately narrow.** Long ball flights only
(`MIN_HORIZON = 15` frames, `MAX_HORIZON = 40` in `config.py`), and

coverage is for leaderboard chasers. A clean comparison beats a broad one
here, and it keeps everything on a laptop.

**Compute is unresolved and does not need resolving.** Tier 0 and most of
Tier 1 run on a laptop given the narrow subset. Tier 2 is where cloud is
needed, and by then the question will answer itself.

**Football knowledge is not required and is not a weakness.** Roy watches
the game but does not know scheme detail (routes, coverages). The chosen
framing does not depend on it — what is needed from the data is geometry:
who is targeted, who is covering, how long the ball is in the air. All
three are columns.

**The 2026 competition data is the working set**, not 2027. The eighth
annual competition ran Sept 2025 – Jan 2026 and is closed; its data,
solutions and discussion are all public, which is worth more than a live
leaderboard. The ninth (2027) had not been announced as of 2026-09-20 and
is expected imminently. When it opens, this pipeline should transfer with
minor schema edits.

section: Things that were considered and rejected
text:
[CONTEXT.md > Things that were considered and rejected]
**Pure ML-systems / cloud framing (no sensing angle).** Effective for large
tech, close to worthless for wireless employers, and it collapses back into
"a model-training project", which is the thing Roy explicitly did not want.

**Chasing leaderboard rank.** Wrong objective. A good score adds nothing to
either target audience and consumes all the time that the degradation study
needs.

**Writing two differently-framed versions of the project.** Unnecessary —
one set of experiments supports both readings.

**A coverage guard that only gates plots, not tables.**
`config.MIN_COVERAGE = 0.25` existed from Tier 0a onward and was wired
into `plot_error_curves`, which correctly stops drawing a predictor's
line once its coverage drops too low. It was never wired into any
table-producing function. The result: every headline number through
Tier 1 Part 3, including the original "6.40 yd @3s" bar, was reported
bare, and 3s coverage turns out to be 3.5% on the full dataset (4.6% on
week 1) — a number nobody would have quoted as a headline if it had been
printed next to the metric. Rejected as a practice going forward:
`evaluate.summarise()` and `evaluate.summarise_at_step()` now attach
`(n, coverage)` to every horizon column they produce, and no number in
README.md is reported without one. See README.md, "Methodology note: the
coverage guard that only guarded the plots," and `run_tier1_taskn.py`
for the audit that caught it and picked the corrected primary horizon
(1.9s, the largest step at ≥50% coverage). The lesson generalises past
this project: a guard proven correct in one code path is not proven
correct everywhere that path's result gets used.

Two follow-up experiments (1 h timebox), both against the observation

  single-model NIS-calibrated value, optimal for one model covering all
  behaviour, and therefore already permissive enough to absorb real
  cuts) down to 0.3 (clean model separation in `test_imm.py`'s synthetic

velocity well," and `constant_velocity` already sits close to that
problem's ceiling — more filtering machinery mostly can't move it,
because none of these models know where the ball is going. That's most

argument for Tier 1, now demonstrated rather than assumed: a learned
model doesn't need to out-filter physics, it needs to use information

- Acceleration direction is assumed along-track (`a` is a magnitude in the

clean-data baseline. It fires with much more room (+0.830) before K5's error
crosses the best physics baseline, which is the operationally relevant
threshold (the point where you'd actually want to switch predictors, not the
point where K5 first gets slightly worse than itself). The decision that

section: K3 reframed — not four monitoring failures, one model problem
text:
[TIER2A_RESULTS.md > K3 reframed — not four monitoring failures, one model problem]
K3's soft failure sigma is 0.00276 — below the published data's own
quantization step (0.01 yd, measured directly; see PART1_DETAIL.md's
methodology note). The data itself can't resolve a position change smaller
than 0.01 yd, and K3 has already failed by a factor of ~3.6x below that
resolution. No signal built on statistical detection can fire before a
real distributional shift exists to detect; at sigma=0.003 nothing has
moved enough to be measurable by any of the four constructions. This isn't
a monitoring gap, it's a model problem.

Confirmed by an independent calculation, not just restated: K3's velocity
gain (8.78) times the differencing amplification (sqrt(2)/dt ~= 14.14)
times sigma=0.003 gives an expected output perturbation of

    8.78 x 14.14 x 0.003 = 0.3725 yd

against a 10%-of-clean-error budget of 1.80 x 0.10 = 0.18 yd. 0.3725 > 0.18
— the arithmetic independently reproduces the empirically-measured failure
point (0.00276) from the gain and amplification numbers established
earlier in Tier 2, without reference to the monitoring signals at all.

**The conclusion for K3: monitoring cannot cover for a model this fragile.
The model has to be fixed (K4's cleaner input, or K5's noise-augmented
training) before deployment, not instrumented around.**
